summary.text: A 45-year-old gentleman, an active smoker (>30 pack years) with a past medical history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and bronchial asthma, presented with sudden onset of central chest pain with diaphoresis and shortness of breath. He arrived at the emergency department of a district hospital within 2 hours from the onset of chest pain. At presentation his blood pressure was 84/48 mmHg, heart rate 43 bpm, oxygen saturation 100% under room air and pain score 10/10, and he was afebrile.

The left sided ECG showed complete heart block with ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF and ST depression in V1 and V2, and the chest X-ray was reported as a rotated film. A diagnosis of inferoposterior STEMI was made. He was given aspirin, clopidogrel, simvastatin, enoxaparin and tenecteplase, with fentanyl and morphine.

One hour after thrombolysis his pain score reduced to 5/10. Blood pressure was 133/94 mmHg without inotropes, heart rate 75 bpm and SaO2 100%, and the left sided ECG showed resolution of complete heart block with less than 50% resolution of ST elevation. He was immediately transferred to a cardiology centre for rescue PCI and arrived 3 hours later.

CK-MB was 273.5 ng/ml, creatinine kinase >4267 IU/ml and serum creatinine 87 umol/L. Coronary angiography was done via a right trans-radial approach; the operator noticed dextrocardia under fluoroscopy and the diagnostic catheter was unable to engage both the left and right coronary arteries, and a decision was made to convert to a trans-femoral approach using JL4 and JR4 catheters. The morphological left coronary artery was normal, with an ulcerated plaque in the proximal RCA and thrombus in the distal RCA, PLV and PDA branches.

A decision was made not to perform PCI of the proximal RCA lesion as he had TIMI 3 flow in the RCA; IV tirofiban was started to treat the distal thrombus and he was observed in the coronary care unit. He was married for 10 years without children, and he had situs inversus that was undiagnosed before this STEMI event. He was discharged well after 4 days with an appointment for outpatient cardiac rehabilitation and intensive cardiovascular risk factors modification.
